analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal to bypass copy protection on digital media and shields internet providers from liability for users' piracy.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 99-0 on May 14, 1998, then folded its text into H.R. 2281, which became the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill implements two 1996 international copyright treaties and writes new rules for the digital age. It makes it a civil violation and, for commercial gain, a crime to break the technological locks on copyrighted works or to build tools that break them. It also gives internet service providers a 'safe harbor' from lawsuits over their users' piracy if they follow a notice-and-takedown process, and it adds small exemptions for libraries, machine repair, and software compatibility.
analysis.who_benefits: Copyright owners — record labels, movie studios, and software companies — gain a new private right of action against anyone who circumvents digital locks, with statutory damages of $200 to $2,500 per violation and criminal penalties up to $500,000 and five years for commercial-scale violations [S4]. They also gain restored copyright protection for foreign sound recordings [S2]. Internet service providers gain near-total protection from money damages for infringement by their users, so long as they remove material on notice and terminate repeat infringers [S4]. Libraries and archives gain the right to make three preservation copies instead of one and a narrow exception to examine locked works before purchase [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Record labels, studios, software firms, and internet providers

how_it_helps.text: Bans circumventing technological protection measures that control access to copyrighted works, and bans making or trafficking in tools designed to circumvent them, backed by civil damages of $200–$2,500 per violation and criminal fines up to $500,000 and five years' imprisonment for willful violations for commercial advantage [S4].

Shields service providers from monetary liability for transmitting, caching, storing, or linking to infringing user content, provided they register a copyright agent, respond to takedown notices, adopt a repeat-infringer termination policy, and accommodate standard technical measures [S4].

Gives libraries and archives three copies (up from one) for preservation, security, or replacement, and lets nonprofit libraries and educational institutions bypass a digital lock solely to decide whether to acquire a commercially available work [S4].

Clarifies that copying a program by activating a machine for maintenance or repair is not infringement, and adds an exception to allow analyzing programs to make independent software interoperable [S4].
Extends U.S. copyright protection to sound recordings first fixed in treaty countries and expands the definition of eligible countries for restored works [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People who use digital media and technology. The circumvention ban makes bypassing a digital lock illegal even when the underlying use — copying a passage for criticism, research on security flaws, backup of a purchased work — would be lawful 'fair use', because the bill's savings clause preserves fair use on paper but provides no right to circumvent a lock in order to exercise it [S4]. Violations carry per-act statutory damages and trafficking bans that cover tools with substantial lawful uses [S4]. Subscribers also face a notice-and-takedown system in which material is removed first on a rightsholder's signed claim, with the burden of a counter-notice falling on the user [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Users of digital media, researchers, and internet subscribers

drawbacks.text: The circumvention ban separates the lock from the copyright: bypassing a digital lock is unlawful even for a use that would be fair use, and the only exemptions are narrow ones for nonprofit libraries making acquisition decisions, law enforcement, and software interoperability [S4].

The trafficking ban reaches any technology 'primarily designed' for circumvention or with 'only limited commercially significant' other uses, exposing toolmakers and security researchers to liability and impoundment of their products [S4].

Notice-and-takedown allows a copyright owner to have material removed on a good-faith assertion, with the burden of filing a counter-notice — under penalty of perjury, consenting to federal court jurisdiction — on the person whose material was taken down [S4].
Copyright owners gained these protections through international treaty commitments, so Congress was ratifying negotiated obligations rather than weighing the rules fresh against alternatives [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safe harbor for service providers is the strongest part for ordinary people: it let internet companies host user content without facing ruinous lawsuits, and is widely credited with enabling the open, user-generated internet. The circumvention regime is the heaviest cost: it created a layer of digital-locks law that outlived its original piracy context and has been used against security research, device repair, and interoperability. The bill handed its largest, most durable wins to two concentrated industries — content owners and service providers — while giving users narrow, condition-laden exemptions. On balance, the bill's design favors concentrated interests, and the public got a genuinely mixed deal.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed the bill 99-0 in May 1998, then in September folded its text into the House bill H.R. 2281 and passed that instead, vitiated its own passage of S. 2037, and laid S. 2037 aside; the DMCA became law through H.R. 2281 that October.

narrative.text: The Senate Judiciary Committee ordered an original measure on April 30, 1998, and Chairman Hatch reported it to the Senate without written report on May 6 [S6].
The Senate passed the bill with an amendment by a 99-0 roll-call vote on May 14, 1998, with all 55 Republicans and all 45 Democrats present voting yes [S7].

On September 17, 1998, the Senate incorporated this measure in H.R. 2281 as an amendment, passed H.R. 2281 in lieu of this measure by unanimous consent, vitiated its previous passage of S. 2037, and indefinitely postponed S. 2037 [S6].
The Senate Judiciary report on the bill carried additional views, and no senator voted against passage [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Copyright owners — the record, film, and software industries — gained the anti-circumvention regime they had sought, and internet service providers gained the safe harbor that became the legal foundation of the user-generated internet. Ordinary users got the open-platform internet the safe harbor made possible, but lost the legal ability to bypass digital locks on works they legitimately own.

for.name: Orrin Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-UT), Chairman, Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, reported the original measure from the Judiciary Committee, and managed it to 99-0 Senate passage five business days after introduction.

for.name: Recording, film, and software industries
for.role: Copyright owners seeking treaty implementation and anti-piracy law
for.what_they_did: Pushed for implementing the 1996 WIPO treaties with a ban on circumventing digital locks; the bill's text tracks their requests closely.

against.name: Library, education, and digital-rights advocates
against.role: Public-interest and library organizations active in the 1998 copyright debate
against.what_they_did: Objected that the circumvention ban would reach lawful uses such as fair use, research, and preservation; won only narrow carve-outs for nonprofit libraries, archives, and interoperability.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee minority views
against.role: Senators filing additional views on the committee report
against.what_they_did: Filed additional views alongside the committee report on the original measure.

sides.party_line_note: There was no partisan divide: the Senate passed it 99-0, with all 55 Republicans and all 45 Democrats voting yes, and no senator voting no [S7].

industries.industry: Music, film, and software publishers (copyright owners)
industries.note: The bill gives them a new cause of action against bypassing digital locks, with per-violation statutory damages and criminal penalties, plus restored rights in foreign sound recordings [S4]. The lock travels with the work, so the industry gains control over what buyers can do with lawfully purchased media — limiting resale, research, and repair — beyond what traditional copyright enforcement required [S4].

industries.industry: Internet service providers and online platforms
industries.note: The safe harbor makes service providers the permanent, legally protected channel for user-uploaded content in exchange for running the notice-and-takedown system and terminating repeat infringers [S4]. This entrenchment is the part of the bill that most clearly served the public: hosting platforms could grow without facing ruinous liability for users' infringement.

They gained three preservation copies instead of one and a narrow pre-purchase exception to digital locks, but digital copies must stay on library premises and the circumvention exemption lasts only long enough to decide whether to buy [S4].
The bill confirms that making a program copy during machine activation for maintenance or repair is not infringement [S4].
